course.title: The Market for "Lemons": Quality Uncertainty and the Market Mechanism
course.level: research paper; read here for a curious beginner with no economics background

units.title: Introduction
units.summary: Sets the question: when buyers judge goods by a market-wide average quality, each seller gains from offering worse goods, so average quality and the size of the market both shrink, and private and social returns diverge.

units.title: The model with automobiles as an example
units.summary: Owners learn whether their car is good or a lemon but buyers cannot tell, so all used cars sell at one price; good cars are withdrawn (a version of Gresham's law). With quality spread evenly between 0 and 2, sellers valuing quality x and buyers 3x/2, the cars offered at price p average p/2, worth only 3p/4 to buyers, so no trade happens at any price even though every trade would benefit both sides; with symmetric information all cars trade.

units.title: Examples and applications
units.summary: Applies the lemons principle beyond cars: health insurance for people over 65 (higher premiums attract the sickest applicants), hiring and group statistics, the cost of dishonesty as honest trade being driven out, and high interest rates and managing agencies in credit markets of developing countries.

units.title: Counteracting institutions
units.summary: Institutions that reduce quality uncertainty and so restore trade: guarantees (risk moves to the seller), brand names that let buyers punish bad quality, chains, and licensing or certification such as degrees.

units.title: Conclusion
units.summary: Trust and informal guarantees are preconditions for trade; the difficulty of telling good quality from bad may explain many economic institutions and is an aspect of uncertainty the standard Arrow-Debreu treatment leaves out.
